checks.expected: 0 disagreements over 600 journeys
checks.observed: 0 disagreements
checks.note: The dynamic program is checked against an exhaustive enumeration of every subset of split points. A solver that returns a plausible number is indistinguishable from one that returns the right one.

checks.expected: splitting is worth doing on a minority of journeys
checks.observed: 14.8% of journeys, median saving 18.31% (11.00 GBP)
checks.note: A fare table where splitting always wins, or never does, would make the optimiser look either brilliant or pointless by construction.

checks.expected: median through fare between 5 and 120 GBP
checks.observed: p10 16, median 35, p90 71 GBP
checks.note: An earlier fare table priced 290 miles at 13 GBP, which made the optimiser look excellent by making the inputs impossible.

checks.expected: a clear gain over the ranker being replaced
checks.observed: NDCG@5 against the oracle: 0.6886 for the logging policy against 0.9298 learned
checks.note: The bar is the policy that produced the log, not a random ordering.

checks.expected: position-corrected labels rank closer to what travellers preferred
checks.note: The correction goes into the label, because XGBoost takes ranking weights per query group and not per document.

checks.expected: the naive click metric ranks the corrected model lower
checks.observed: NDCG@5 on clicks 0.3054 for the uncorrected model against 0.2987 for the corrected one, while the oracle says the opposite
checks.note: This is the trap the whole project is about. Judge by held-out clicks and you reject the better ranker, because the clicks were produced by the ranker you are replacing.

checks.expected: the corrected metric agrees with the truth better than the naive one
checks.observed: across 10 candidate rankers, Spearman correlation with the oracle is +0.624 for the naive click metric and +0.988 for the inverse-propensity-corrected one
checks.note: This is what a promotion gate reads, so it is the number that decides which model ships.

checks.expected: no skew when the two sides agree
checks.observed: No skew: 2,158 replayed rows agree on all 21 features.
checks.note: The half everyone forgets. A detector that always fires is one that gets switched off.

checks.expected: exactly advance_days differs
checks.observed: ['advance_days'], largest absolute difference {'advance_days': 1.0}
checks.note: A training job on UTC and a serving host on local time shift every advance window by one. Nothing throws.

checks.expected: exactly seats_remaining differs
checks.observed: ['seats_remaining'], 375 rows of 2,158
checks.note: The fill is a statistic of the training set. A serving process that recomputes it drifts away from the value the model was fitted on.

checks.expected: the as-of filter materially changes the value
checks.observed: 100.0% of 6,515 rows differ, mean absolute difference 0.28143, 5,791 rows have no trailing window yet
checks.note: Dropping the date filter is one line and it is the difference between a feature and a leak.

checks.expected: the leaky model wins on held-out clicks, which is the only offline metric a real team has
checks.observed: NDCG@5 on clicks 0.3088 honest against 0.4107 leaky; on the oracle the order is reversed, 0.9326 against 0.8827
checks.note: final_load_factor is the same column as load_factor_at_search read after the train had gone, so it carries the click it is being used to predict. It wins on the click metric and loses on the truth, which is precisely why a leak survives review.

checks.expected: and collapses once the column is unavailable at serving time
checks.observed: 0.8827 offline collapses to 0.7809 in production, a drop of 11.5%
checks.note: The offline number is the one that would have been used to decide.

checks.expected: p99 at or under 25.0 ms
checks.observed: p50 0.621 ms, p99 0.924 ms over 600 searches (96.3% headroom)
checks.note: A better model that cannot answer in time is not a better model.

checks.expected: loading raises when the recorded feature order differs
checks.observed: raised
checks.note: A model trained before a feature was inserted scores against the wrong columns and raises nothing at all.

checks.expected: p99 at or under 25 ms end to end, all responses 200

checks.observed: shifted: ['seats_remaining']; worst by population stability index [('seats_remaining', 0.54358), ('price_gbp', 0.04769), ('price_over_route_median_7d', 0.03583)]
checks.note: No nulls, no schema change, no row-count change, every value a legal integer. Freshness and null-rate checks stay green throughout.

checks.expected: no alerts when a sample is compared with itself
checks.observed: 0 alerts, worst PSI 0.00087
checks.note: Split at random from one period, so any alert here is a false one.

checks.expected: population stability index below 0.1 on price_gbp despite a planted 0.42% daily fare trend
checks.observed: price_gbp PSI 0.0477 over 45 days, which the bands call 'stable'
checks.note: Reported as a limitation, not hidden. PSI compares binned shares, so a slow location shift inside a wide distribution moves very little mass across quantile edges. A trend needs a trend test -- a Mann-Kendall on the daily mean -- and a monitor that only computes PSI will not see one of the two most common ways a feature goes wrong.

checks.expected: owner, severity and first action on every alert
checks.observed: 1 alerts, owners ['ml-platform']
checks.note: An alert nobody owns is a notification.

checks.observed: 11 resources, 9 variables, 3 outputs across ['main.tf']; problems: []

planted.logging_policy: sort by price ascending with gaussian noise (sd 0.55); ignores duration, changes and departure time entirely
planted.leak: final_load_factor is known only after the train has gone and rises with how appealing the journey was, so it encodes the label. load_factor_at_search is the same column read as of the search, and is legitimate.
planted.notes: true_utility is an oracle column. No click log has it. It exists so a ranker can be scored against what the traveller would actually have preferred, rather than against the log produced by the ranker being replaced.

propensities.note: Estimated only on searches shown in a randomised order. In ordinary traffic position and preference are correlated by design -- that is what a ranker is -- so a curve fitted there would remove the signal along with the bias.

alerts.subject: seats_remaining
alerts.summary: `seats_remaining` has a population stability index of 0.544 against the training distribution, above the 0.25 threshold. Nothing is missing and no row count changed; the values have moved.
alerts.runbook: Compare the drifted feature against its upstream source before retraining. A shift caused by a producer change is a bug to fix; a shift caused by the world moving is a reason to retrain, and retraining on the first one bakes the bug into the model.
